stories.text: Queen Elizabeth II opened the Queen's Medical Centre on 28 July 1977, and it took its first patient the next year. It was the first hospital in the UK built to be a teaching hospital, with the University of Nottingham's medical and nursing schools on the same site, and with more than 1,300 beds it was long the largest hospital in the country.

aka: Priory Church of St. Anthony, Lenton

stories.text: Henry II gave Lenton Priory an eight-day fair for St Martin's Day, which Henry III lengthened to twelve, with tolls paid to the monks for every booth. The fair outlived the priory: in 1584, when servants of Mary, Queen of Scots came, it was a horse fair, and by the 17th century it was known as a great fair for all sorts of horses. In the 19th century farmers and horse dealers still came.

William Peverel founded a priory of Cluniac monks at Lenton in about 1102–08, and richly endowed it. In February 1538 its last prior, Nicholas Heath, and many of his monks were thrown into prison, accused of high treason. The prior, eight monks and four Lenton labourers were executed, in Nottingham and in front of the priory, and the priory was dissolved that year. Little is left: the Priory Church of St Anthony is thought to keep part of its hospital chapel.

stories.text: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) maps the brain at work from the tiny magnetic fields its cells make, but its scanners weighed about half a tonne, because their sensors had to be kept at −269 °C, and the patient had to keep still. In March 2018 researchers at the Sir Peter Mansfield Imaging Centre, with UCL, showed in Nature a scanner worn like a helmet, built from new "quantum" sensors in a 3D-printed shell.[^uon] Wearing it, people could nod, stretch, drink tea and even play ping pong while their brains were scanned.[^ucl]

stories.text: Peter Mansfield came to the University of Nottingham in 1964 and developed magnetic resonance imaging here. Just before Christmas 1978 a full-body scanner was installed, and he made the first scan of a live patient. He shared the Nobel Prize in 2003 with Paul Lauterbur.
